verse_quote: I stood beside him and killed him.
note:
In light of 1 Sam. 31:4–6, it seems probable that the Amalekite happened upon Saul’s body before the Philistines and, in the hopes of receiving a reward from David, has fabricated a part for himself in Saul’s death. Others have suggested that Saul’s act of falling on his sword might only have wounded him and that the Amalekite’s account is therefore plausible. In either case, the Amalekite expects to receive a different response from David than what he actually receives.

The way in which Saul’s regalia come into David’s possession is a stark contrast to Jonathan’s voluntary surrender of his robe and weapons to David (1 Sam. 18:4 and note). This contrast epitomizes the radically different responses of Saul and Jonathan to the divine will with respect to David and the house of Saul (e.g., 1 Sam. 18:28, 29; 19:4; 20:30, 31; 23:17, 18).
The Amalekite is clearly subject to the laws of Israel because he is an alien who resides in the land of Israel (Lev. 19:33, 34; 24:22).

The second section (vv. 25, 26) expresses David’s personal mourning for Jonathan. The lament closes with a final repetition of the mournful refrain.

David’s praise of Jonathan’s love (cf. 1 Sam. 18:3) does not mean that love between friends is inherently superior to marital love. Rather, the point seems to be the astonishingly selfless quality of Jonathan’s love for David. David himself does not prove selfless in his relations with women (3:2 note). Modern attempts to find in this verse evidence for a homosexual relationship between Jonathan and Saul have no exegetical warrant. Sadly, many people in our hyper-sexualized culture find it inconceivable that people of the same gender can have deep, loving friendships with one another without transgressing boundaries into sexual intimacy. Scripture, however, frequently extols the bonds of brotherhood and sisterhood, friendships that exhibit sacrificial love without any hint of eroticism (Prov. 17:17; 18:24; 4:9–12).

**Hebron.** Located nineteen miles (31 km) southwest of Jerusalem, Hebron has the highest elevation of any town in Israel and is strategically well suited for the inauguration of David’s rule over Judah. Hebron was a Canaanite royal city when the Israelites came from Egypt (Josh. 10:3), but its links with the people of God extend back to the patriarchs (e.g., Gen. 13:18; 23:2, 19; 35:27). Under Israelite rule, it becomes both a Levitical city and a city of refuge (Josh. 21:11–13).

As will become apparent, this last surviving son of Saul is little more than a pawn in the hands of Abner.

note: At least in the northern tribes, the transfer of power to David after the death of Saul is not unopposed. But the tide is running in David’s favor (2:30, 31 note).

The list of six sons born to David (vv. 2–5) amplifies the statement in v. 1 that “David grew stronger and stronger,” while the wrangling between Abner and Ish-bosheth over a concubine (vv. 6–11) dramatizes the final statement in v. 1 that “the house of Saul became weaker and weaker.”

**3:2 sons were born to David at Hebron.** As the list that follows reveals, David takes additional wives in Hebron. In 5:13–16, after David’s arrival in Jerusalem, yet more wives and concubines are added, and at least eleven more children are born to David (cf. 1 Chr. 3:1–9). While the narrator offers no explicit evaluation of David’s behavior (ancient Near Eastern kings commonly multiplied wives and children), it violates the standards of Deut. 17:17.

verse_quote: Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur.
note: David’s marrying a foreign wife from the small Aramean kingdom of Geshur may be politically motivated, giving him an ally north of Ish-bosheth’s shaky realm.

verse_quote: Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine.
note: Abner’s appropriation of Saul’s concubine amounts to a claim on the throne (12:8 note; 16:21 note; 1 Kin. 2:22). The reader is not told whether Ish-bosheth’s suspicion is well-founded or simple paranoia. Whatever the case, Abner uses the accusation as an occasion to shift his allegiance to David (vv. 8–10).

verse_quote: what the LORD has sworn to him.

note: A proverbial expression for the whole country (Judg. 20:1).
Ish-bosheth’s reaction indicates that Abner is in a position not only to make a threat but also to carry it out.

verse_quote: To whom does the land belong.
note: Abner means either that the land is his own, as one who controls it and can give it to David, or that the land is David’s by right, and that David should enlist Abner’s help to secure it.

The insecurity of Ish-bosheth’s position is evident not only in his fear of Abner (v. 11) but also in his inability to resist David’s orders.

Num. 35:16–25; Deut. 19:11–13; Josh. 20:3). Joab may also want to eliminate a potential rival in David’s court (see his murder of Amasa in 20:10).

note: David’s decision only to utter a curse upon Joab’s house rather than take direct disciplinary action may be a result of the ambiguous circumstances of Joab’s crime. More likely, however, such factors as Joab’s considerable power and reputation, and his familial relationship with David influence his decision. Israel, on the other hand, is “dismayed” by what seems to be a rejection of their friendly overture to David (3:17–21).

A city of great antiquity (occupied as early as the third millennium B.C..), Jerusalem is in the tribal region of Benjamin, near the northern border of Judah. The city is mentioned in extrabiblical texts as early as the twentieth century B.C. in Egypt. The city was earlier conquered by Judah (Judg. 1:8), but neither Judah nor Benjamin have been successful in permanently dislodging its Jebusite inhabi­tants (Josh. 15:63; Judg. 1:21). David may well think that Jerusalem’s strategic location and relatively independent status makes the city well suited to the establishment of a national capital that will not imply favoritism to any particular region.

**Jebusites ... said to David.** The Jebusites’ taunt, whether suggestive of overconfidence or simply of a determination to fight to the last man (even be he blind or lame), reflects the hostility between the Jebusites and David (see v. 8; 1 Sam. 17:54 note).

This marks the first occurrence of “Zion” in the Bible and the only one in Samuel. The name originally designated a fortified mound located at the southern end of the Ophel ridge. Eventually, the name came to be used in an extended sense for all of Jerusalem (2 Kin. 19:21; Is. 2:3) and even for the entire nation of Israel (Ps. 149:2; Is. 46:13). The name occurs frequently in Israel’s poetic and prophetic literature, where it is often presented as the place of God’s mighty acts of salvation and judgment (e.g., Ps. 14:7; Is. 4:4; Lam. 4:11).

Archaeologists have uncovered the remains of a complex water system in Jerusalem; it was built to bring water into the settlement from the Gihon Spring that was located outside of the city. This may be the shaft that Joab and his men use to penetrate the city (1 Chr. 11:6).
Heb. “fill.” It perhaps refers to terraces that support buildings on top of them. It is mentioned in numerous passages (Judg. 9:6, 20; 1 Kin. 9:15, 24; 11:27; 1 Chr. 11:8; 2 Chr. 32:5).

Just as chs. 3, 4 detail how “the house of Saul became weaker and weaker” (3:1; 3:2–11 note), so chs. 5–10 show David growing “stronger and stronger” (3:1). The fundamental reason for David’s success is that the Lord is with him (1 Sam. 16:18 note).

In David’s time, Tyre is a Phoenician port city about thirty-five miles (56 km) north of Mount Carmel and twenty-five miles (40 km) south of Sidon. Hiram’s generosity to David may be motivated by the impressiveness of David’s recent accomplishments, but it also involves an element of self-interest. Tyre needs the inland trade routes controlled by David and the agricultural produce of central Palestine (cf. Ezra 3:7). Hiram’s friendship with Israel continues well into Solomon’s reign (1 Kin. 5:1–12; 9:11).

**Uzzah and Ahio.** While attempts have been made to identify Uzzah with Eleazar in 1 Sam. 7:1, it is more likely that the two sons mentioned here are brothers of Eleazar, or possibly even grandsons of Abinadab. The Hebrew word “son” can also mean “descendant.”

Mentioned here for the first time, Nathan the prophet will also play a significant role in ch. 12 and 1 Kin. 1. See also 1 Chr. 29:29; 2 Chr. 9:29; 29:25.

**in a tent.** David apparently views his palace as symbolic of his now-established rule (5:11, 12), and he proposes that God’s rule should be similarly symbolized with a permanent dwelling.

The theological and historical significance of the divine promise to David recorded in these verses (par. 1 Chr. 17:3–15) can hardly be overestimated. Indeed, the promise of an enduring Davidic kingdom has been called the summit of the entire OT. Looking back, it takes up the promises of blessing made to Abraham and his elect seed (Gen. 17:16) and brings them to rest on David (vv. 9, 10, 12). Looking forward, it prepares for the messianic hope that inspires Israel’s faith before and after the exile in Babylon (Is. 11:1; Jer. 23:5, 6; Zech. 3:8; 6:12). The hope for a Messiah culminates in the coming of Jesus Christ (Is. 9:1–7; Luke 1:32, 33, 69, 70; Acts 2:30, 31; 13:22, 23; Rom. 1:1–4; 2 Tim. 2:8; Rev. 22:16).

Cf. 3:18; Ps. 89:3. The Lord’s reference to David as “my servant” places him in a select company that includes Abraham (Gen. 26:24), Moses (Num. 12:7, 8; Deut. 34:5), Caleb (Num. 14:24), and Joshua (Josh. 24:29).

verse_quote: I have not lived in a house.
note: God has accompanied His elect people throughout their wanderings (vv. 6, 7). Not until He has planted them in their place (v. 10) and they enjoy “rest” (v. 11) that exceeds what they already have under David (v. 1) will He allow a permanent house to be built for His name (v. 13).

See note on 1 Sam. 16:18.

**a great name.** The declaration of a great name recalls the divine promise made to the patriarch Abraham in Gen. 12:2. Cf. 8:13, where David “made a name for himself,” possibly an implied criticism because David promotes his own name (on promoting one’s name, cf. Gen. 11:4).

verse_quote: the LORD will make you a house.
note: Having declined David’s offer to build Him a house (i.e., a temple; v. 5), the Lord counters with the gracious announcement that He will instead establish a house (i.e., a dynasty) for David.

A double prophecy that is first fulfilled in Solomon, but the everlasting nature of David’s throne finds its culmination in the Messiah (see Acts 2:30).

**who shall come from your body.** The same words were spoken to Abraham in Gen. 15:4.

It was “for his great name’s sake” that the Lord refused to reject His people after their sinful request for a king (1 Sam. 12:22). Now He announces to David that his own son, who will succeed him as king, will build a temple “for my name.” For an explication of the significance of God’s name, see Ex. 34:5–7 and note on 1 Sam. 17:45.

The full significance of this promise, expressive of the special relationship that the Lord establishes with the Davidic kings (Pss. 2:7; 89:18–37), is ultimately realized in Christ (Mark 1:11; Acts 13:33; Heb. 1:5).

**7:14 I will discipline him.** As a father, the Lord will discipline the royal son when he does wrong, but His covenantal love will never be taken away from David’s line. Though the punishment is severe, extending even to the loss of land and temple (1 Kin. 9:6–9), God’s promise to establish forever the throne of David cannot fail. This promise will increasingly come to be understood in messianic terms (Is. 9:7; 11:1–5; Jer. 33:14–26; Mic. 5:2–5).

verse_quote: David went in and sat before the
note:
LORD**.** Presumably David sits in front of the ark, the symbol of the Lord’s presence (Ex. 25:22; 30:6; Deut. 10:8; Josh. 6:8). In this era, it is not usual to sit while praying (Deut. 10:8).

**Who am I.** Having offered God a house (i.e., a temple), David is overwhelmed by the Lord’s declaration that He will build David a house (i.e., a dynasty). The humility evident in David’s “Who am I” agrees with his recognition that it is the sovereign Lord who has been with him (1 Sam. 16:18 note) to bring him this far.

This phrase is difficult to interpret. The parallel at 1 Chr. 17:17 reads quite differently: “[you] have shown me future generations.” The likely sense is, “this is for the benefit of mankind.” Like the covenant with Abraham (Gen. 12:1–3) and like the purpose of the crossing of the Red Sea (Ps. 66:5, 6), the covenant with David has implications for all humanity.

David is moved by consideration of his unique status and that of his house (vv. 18–21) to contemplate the uniqueness of his God. He is the only true God, and in His unmerited favor He has chosen David and the nation of Israel itself to be the people through whom His great name will become known (Ex. 15:11–13; Deut. 7:6–8).

verse_quote: David defeated the Philistines and subdued them.
note:
In this summary of David’s victories, pride of place is given to his defeat of the Philistines, Israel’s archenemy (3:18; 1 Sam. 9:16) and against whom David’s successes far surpass those of his predecessor, Saul (1 Sam. 14:52). See note on 5:25.

**Metheg-ammah.** The name is otherwise unattested.

David executes two-thirds of his Moabite opponents and reduces the survivors to tributary status. The cause of David’s ruthless treatment of a people whom he earlier trusted (1 Sam. 22:3) is not stated.

**Moabites.** See notes on 1 Sam. 22:3. David’s great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite (Ruth 4:21, 22).

This name appears to be a compound of “Hadad,” the Syrian storm-god or Baal, and “ezer,” meaning “help.” “Hadad” is found elsewhere in compound names of Syrian monarchs (1 Kin. 15:18). Though defeated by David, Hadadezer later assists the Ammonites in their opposition to David (10:15–19).

**Zobah.** Already during Saul’s reign there was conflict between Israel and the “kings of Zobah” (1 Sam. 14:47), a Syrian region north of Israel.
David did this to the horses so that they would be of no further military use. See also the numbers given in the parallel passage of 1 Chr. 18:4.

verse_quote: the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
note: This statement, repeated in v. 14, sets the summary of David’s victories apart from that of Saul’s (1 Sam. 14:47–51; 16:18 and notes). The Lord is the source of David’s conquests.
1 Chr. 18:8 notes that Solomon uses this bronze in the construction of the temple.
A region in Syria to the east of Zobah (8:3) and west of the Euphrates River Valley.

verse_quote: These also King David dedicated to the
note: LORD**.** David’s action is perhaps in preparation for the temple to be built by Solomon (cf. 1 Chr. 22:1–5, 14; 29:1–5, 16–19).

The slaughter of eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt is credited to Abishai in 1 Chr. 18:12. It may be that Abishai receives credit as one of David’s generals, possibly to remove the implied criticism of David, who makes a name for himself. See also Ps. 60 and its title.

verse_quote: the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
note: This clause repeats v. 6, and it highlights the theme of the chapter.

As the prototypical theocratic king, David subjugates Israel’s enemies (vv. 1–14), but he knows that he is called to be just (23:3). His descendants do not always follow his example, despite prophetic exhortation (Jer. 22:3).

**to all his people.** See note on 5:12.

See note on 2:18.

**recorder.** The specific nature of this office is hard to determine. Conjectures include keeper of state records, secretary of state, or royal herald.

Zadok is a Levite priest descended from Aaron through Eleazar (1 Chr. 6:3–8, 50–53). He becomes the sole high priest in Solomon’s administration (1 Kin. 2:35). From that time on, the Zadokite priests form one of the most important and influential priestly families (Ezra 7:1, 2; Ezek. 40:46; 44:15).

**Ahimelech the son of Abiathar.** According to 20:25 and 1 Kin. 4:4, Zadok and Abiathar are David’s priests (see 15:24, 35; 19:11). It was earlier reported that Abiathar, “one of the sons of Abim­elech,” joined David during his exile from Saul’s court (1 Sam. 22:20). It seems likely, therefore, that the names of father and son have somehow been reversed here (as also in 1 Chr. 18:16). Abiathar is a descendant of Eli through an Ahitub different from Zadok’s father (1 Sam. 14:3; 22:20). His removal by Solomon for having supported Adonijah’s bid for the throne (1 Kin. 1:7, 8) brings to final fulfillment the judgment on the house of Eli (1 Sam. 2:31 note; 1 Kin. 2:26, 27).

**Seraiah was secretary.** Variations in the recording of this name (20:25; 1 Chr. 18:16; possibly 1 Kin. 4:3) may suggest a non-Israelite origin—perhaps Egypt, where the scribal tradition was well established. The scribe was among the highest ranking civil servants (2 Kin. 12:10; 18:18).

A man of outstanding military credentials (23:20–22), Benaiah demonstrates his intense loyalty to David and Solomon (1 Kin. 1:8, 36, 37), and, after carrying out Solomon’s order to execute Joab, becomes commander-in-chief of Solomon’s army (1 Kin. 2:34, 35; 4:4).

**Cherethites and the Pelethites.** See note on 1 Sam. 30:14.

**priests.** This is an office for which they are not clearly eligible. The parallel at 1 Chr. 18:17 reads “chief officials in the service of the king.” David and Solomon at least supervise sacrifices (6:17, 18; 1 Chr. 21:28; 2 Chr. 5:6).

On the progressive decline of the “house of Saul,” see note on 5:10. David promised Saul that he would not wipe out his posterity (1 Sam. 24:21, 22).

**kindness for Jonathan’s sake.** On the covenant between David and Jonathan, see 1 Sam. 18:3, 4; 20:15 and notes.
He had been a servant in the house of Saul, but now he says to David, “I am your servant.” He comes back into the story in 16:1–4 and 19:16–30.

Mentioned also in 17:27–29, Machir appears to have been a wealthy man in a good position to host a descendant of Israel’s first king.

**Lo-debar.** This city has been tentatively located in Gilead about four miles (6 km) northwest of Mahanaim, Ish-bosheth’s short-lived capital east of the Jordan River (2:8 note), and ten miles (16 km) south of the Sea of Galilee.
See note on 4:4.

The property that David restores to Mephibosheth may well be substantial (v. 10 note).

**you shall eat at my table.** David also offers Mephibosheth a place of honor at his own table (on the practice, see 2 Kin. 25:29). It has been suggested that David’s act is somewhat self-serving, since the arrangement enables him to keep Mephibosheth under surveillance. But this suggestion is unlikely for several reasons. The text offers no hint of such a motive; Mephibosheth’s crippled condition makes him less of a threat; and David surely knows from experience that it is dangerous for a rival to be at the king’s court (cf. 16:3, 15–23).
See note on 1 Sam. 24:14.
The number of men put to work farming the land shows that the properties are extensive. The number also indicates Ziba’s power and his potential threat to Mephibosheth (16:3; 19:26).

verse_quote: a young son, whose name was Mica.
note: See also the genealogies of 1 Chr. 8:34, 35; 9:40, 41. David’s beneficence “for Jonathan’s sake” (v. 1) is not limited to Mephibosheth.
See note on 1 Sam. 11:1.

verse_quote: I will deal loyally with Hanun the son of Nahash.
note: The Hebrew phrase translated “deal loyally” suggests that there is a covenant between David and Nahash, even though Nahash’s aggression toward Israel had helped Saul rise to power (1 Sam. 11:1–11; 12:12). The friendly relationship between David and Nahash may have been established during the period when David was a fugitive from Saul.
Presumably this is a reference to the capital city, Rabbah (11:1 note).
Hanun humiliates the emissaries.
The first site west of the Jordan and just north of the Dead Sea that will be reached by the delegation returning from Rabbah.

verse_quote: the Syrians of Beth-rehob ... of Zobah.
note:
See note on 8:3. Beth-rehob lies southwest of Zobah (cf. Num. 13:21; Judg. 18:28).

**Maacah.** Maacah is the region just north of Lake Huleh (Deut. 3:14; Josh. 13:11–13), which is just north of the Sea of Galilee.

**Tob.** A city east of the Jordan River and forty-eight miles (77 km) north of Rabbah (11:1 note; cf. Judg. 11:3, 5).
See note on 2:18.
Israel’s army is in a vise; the Ammonite forces are arrayed outside of Rabbah on one side of Israel, and the Syrian forces are on the other side.
See note on 2:18.

verse_quote: Be of good courage ... may the LORD do what seems good to him.
note: Finding himself in the difficult military position of having to fight on two fronts, Joab urges courage but recognizes that the outcome of the conflict will depend ultimately on the Lord (cf. David’s words in 15:26).
Apparently he does not capture the city of Rabbah on this occasion (11:1; 12:26–29).

See note on 8:3.

**Helam.** About twelve miles (19 km) north of Tob (v. 6 note).

verse_quote: the Syrians were afraid to save.
note: The door is opened to a second campaign against the Ammonites.

verse_quote: when kings go out to battle.
note:
See 1 Kin. 20:22, 26. In the Near East, spring was a logical time for military campaigns; the winter rains had ceased and the labor-intensive harvest had begun, so there was grain in the fields for consumption.

**David sent Joab.** This is not the first time that David has sent Joab on a military expedition (10:7), but since it is the time when “kings go out to battle” and “David remained at Jerusalem,” there may be some criticism of David for staying behind.

**besieged Rabbah.** Called “Rabbah of the Ammonites” in Deut. 3:11 and elsewhere (12:26; 17:27; Jer. 49:2; Ezek. 21:20), this city was the capital of Ammon (Amos 1:13–15). It is twenty-four miles (38.6 km) east of the Jordan River opposite Jericho. In NT times it was called Philadelphia, and today it is Amman, Jordan. See also 10:14 and note.

verse_quote: late one afternoon ... David arose from his couch.
note: David’s luxury is in marked contrast to the activities of Joab and his men (vv. 1, 11).

Not until 12:24 will the name “Bathsheba” be mentioned again; in the intervening verses the reference is to “the woman” (v. 5) or to “the wife of Uriah” (v. 26; 12:10, 15). The focus is not on Bathsheba herself so much as on her status as the wife of another man.

**Eliam.** If Bathsheba’s father is the same as “Eliam the son of Ahithophel” (23:34), this might help to explain Ahithophel’s later betrayal of David in favor of Absalom’s conspiracy (15:12; 16:15), which ostensibly is motivated by a sense of David’s failure to provide justice for the people (15:4, 6). Notice especially the nature of Ahithophel’s advice in 16:20, 21.

**Uriah.** Uriah is a Hebrew name meaning “the LORD is my light.” He is a member one of David’s elite forces called “The Thirty” (23:24–39).
If the reference is to menstruation (Lev. 15:19–30), the point is to remove all doubt that David is responsible for Bathsheba’s pregnancy (v. 5).
Bathsheba leaves it to David to decide what to do.

Uriah understands David to be suggesting that he sleep with his wife. This might make possible the deception that Uriah is the child’s father.

**a present.** David perhaps wants to encourage the couple.

verse_quote: But Uriah ... did not go down to his house.
note: Despite David’s efforts, Uriah does not do what he considers wrong. It is possible that Uriah knows about David’s relationship with Bathsheba (perhaps from the messengers of v. 4), but this is unlikely in view of his willingness to carry a letter from David to Joab (v. 14). Uriah explains his abstinence in v. 11. Since sexual activity is a source of ritual impurity under the old covenant, obedient soldiers exercise abstinence during a military exercise (1 Sam. 21:5).

verse_quote: The ark and Israel and Judah.
note: Uriah’s insistence that he will not fare better than his fellow combatants again underscores by contrast the reprehensible nature of David’s sin. Even though the Lord Himself (as symbolized by the presence of the ark) is on the field of battle, the king is in Jerusalem (vv. 1, 2 and notes).
See note on v. 8. Uriah still remains faithful to his duty and does not go home.
Having failed to manipulate Uriah, David now feels compelled to take another course, and Joab, not surprisingly (2:18; 3:27; 20:10 and notes), is willing to help.
“Besheth,” meaning “shame,” was sometimes substituted for “Baal.”

verse_quote: all that Joab had sent him.
note: The Septuagint has a longer reading in which this statement is followed by an angry response from David along the lines anticipated by Joab in vv. 20, 21.

verse_quote: Do not let this matter displease you.
note: David’s answer is cynical. He pretends to console his accomplice in murder. Note the similar phrasing of v. 27.

The customary period of mourning for her is probably seven days (Gen. 50:10; 1 Sam. 31:13). National leaders in those days were sometimes mourned for longer periods. Aaron was mourned thirty days (Num. 20:29), likewise Moses (Deut. 34:8). The Egyptians mourned seventy days for Jacob (Gen. 50:3).

**bore him a son.** See 12:14.

**displeased the** LORD**.** Lit. “was evil in the eyes of the LORD”; see v. 25. David has broken at least four of the Ten Commandments: murder, adultery, lying, and coveting his neighbor’s wife (Ex. 20:2–17; Deut. 5:6–21).

The prophets were servants of the word of God, which has authority even over kings. The prophets needed courage and were sometimes in sharp conflict with the kings (1 Kin. 22:8; 2 Kin. 1:3, 4; Mark 6:17; cf. Acts 7:52).

**one rich and the other poor.** The rich man is David, and the poor man is Uriah. A similar injustice is later perpetrated by Ahab and Jezebel against Naboth (1 Kin. 21:1–14).
The verse ends with the Hebrew word for “daughter,” which is also the first syllable of the name “Bathsheba.”

verse_quote: the man who has done this deserves to die.
note: Nathan’s parable has succeeded; in pronouncing judgment on the rich man, David has condemned himself. His response is an exclamation, not a legal decision. He mentions death first, then restitution.

Ex. 22:1 orders fourfold restitution for stolen sheep. Some commentators have detected here a hint of David’s subsequent loss of four sons: the first son of Bathsheba (vv. 14, 18), Amnon (13:28, 29), Absalom (18:14, 15), and Adonijah (1 Kin. 2:24, 25).

In a manner typical of prophetic judgment speeches (1 Sam. 2:27–36 note), Nathan begins with an accusation that includes a description of the Lord’s providence (vv. 7, 8), a question, and an indictment (v. 9). He concludes by announcing the judgment and the penalties corresponding to the crime.

**12:7 I anointed you.** Cf. Samuel’s indictment of Saul (1 Sam. 15:17).

It is uncertain whether this statement is to be taken literally (only one wife and one concubine of Saul are mentioned; 3:7; cf. 1 Sam. 14:50) or as simply referring to the full extent of David’s inheritance of Saul’s kingdom. On the matter of kings acquiring their predecessors’ harems, see 3:7 and note.

This same idiom appears in 11:25, 27.

**You have struck down Uriah.** Because David causes Uriah to die in battle, he is as guilty as if he had murdered him with his own hand.

verse_quote: the sword shall never depart from your house.
note: As Uriah was killed by violence, the house of David will be plagued by violence. Absalom kills Amnon (13:28, 29); Joab kills Absalom (18:14, 15); and Solomon orders the deaths of Adonijah (1 Kin. 2:24, 25) and Joab (1 Kin. 2:29–34). In addition, as David has committed sexual sin, there is sexual sin in his household (2 Sam. 13:1–15).

The prophecy is fulfilled by the rebellion of Absalom (chs. 15–18).

**lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.** This prediction is fulfilled in 16:21, 22.

LORD**.** When charged by God’s prophet, David responds with an immediate and unqualified confession; cf. Saul’s confessions in 1 Sam. 15:24, 25, 30 (notes). Ps. 51, according to its superscription, is a fuller picture of David’s repentance.

**you shall not die.** See notes on 11:5; 12:5.

verse_quote: nor did he eat food with them.
note: See note on 1 Sam. 1:7.

Like Eli, but unlike Saul, David humbly accepts the Lord’s discipline (15:26; 16:11; cf. 1 Sam. 3:18 and notes). His humble response probably explains why his dynasty is established unlike the dynasty of Saul.
That is, in the place of the dead (1 Sam. 28:19 note; Gen. 37:35).

Bathsheba is called David’s wife for the first time (11:3 note). She has been referred to as “the wife of Uriah the Hittite” for most of the story in chs. 11, 12 (11:3, 26; 12:10, 15).

**Solomon.** This name is likely derived from the Hebrew word for “peace” (cf. 1 Chr. 22:9). Another possibility is that it means “replacement”; the birth of Solomon compensates for the loss of the first child.

See text note. This name confirms that “the LORD loved him” (v. 24) and bodes well for the future of the Davidic house. Despite the sin of David and his descendants, the Lord’s favor will not be withdrawn (7:14 note).
The narrative once again returns to the Ammonite campaign (11:1 and note). This time it is not David who sends for Joab, but Joab who sends for David (v. 27).
Joab’s concern may be prompted by an interest in David’s reputation and the propriety of having the king receive the captive crown.

A crown weighing as much as seventy-five pounds (“a talent”) would have been too heavy to wear except for brief ceremonies. The crown could have been from a statue of Milcom or Molech. The same Hebrew letters translated as “their king” can also be read as “Milcom” (i.e., Molech, the chief god of the Ammonites; see 1 Kin. 11:5, 33).
Subjugation of defeated enemies is common practice for David (8:2) and in the culture of the ancient Near East generally (Ex. 1:11; Josh. 9:22–27; 1 Kin. 9:20, 21).

David’s sons follow their father’s example of sexual misconduct (Amnon, vv. 1–22) and murder (Absalom, vv. 23–39).

**13:1** Absalom and Tamar are siblings, having been born to David and his wife Maacah. Amnon is the eldest son of David, and he is a child of Ahinoam; thus Amnon is a half-brother of Tamar.

Both the words used for the “cakes” and their preparation (“make”) are cognates of the Hebrew word for “heart” and may have an amorous connotation. A more common word for food is used by Jonadab in v. 5 and by David in v. 7. Sadly, David seems to miss the innuendo in Amnon’s overture.

**in my sight.** This emphasis (also in vv. 5, 8) is suggestive of a lustful aspect in Amnon’s request.

Tamar’s desperate appeal to Amnon points first to the distinctive moral standards of Israel (“such a thing is not done in Israel,” v. 12), then to the claims of human decency (“my shame”), then to Amnon’s self-interest (“you would be as one of the outrageous fools”), and finally to marriage as a better means of fulfilling Amnon’s desire (v. 13). But he does not listen (v. 14). Incest is immoral in Israel but practiced in the surrounding nations (Lev. 18:1–3, 6).

**13:12 do not violate me.** The verb is used elsewhere to describe acts of rape (Gen. 34:2; Deut. 22:24, 29) and sexual violence (Judg. 19:24; 20:5).

verse_quote: he will not withhold me from you.
note: It is uncertain whether David would allow such a marriage (see Lev. 18:9, 11; 20:17; Deut. 27:22) or whether Tamar is simply trying every possible argument.

verse_quote: the hatred ... was greater than the love.
note: With keen psychological insight, the narrator notes that Amnon no sooner violates Tamar than he is suddenly repulsed by the victim of his crime.

verse_quote: this wrong in sending me away is greater.

note: A rude and abrupt way of referring to Tamar. Cf. Amnon’s terse dismissal of her (v. 15).
A garment of similar description was given to Joseph by his father, Jacob (Gen. 37:3).

verse_quote: Has Amnon your brother been with you.
note:
Absalom’s ability to discern the wrong suffered by Tamar suggests that Amnon’s infatuation with her has not been a deep secret.

**hold your peace ... do not take this to heart.** Though seeking to calm his sister, Absalom will soon seek revenge against Amnon (vv. 22, 32).

That David is furious at Amnon’s violation of Tamar is understandable; that he takes no disciplinary action is not (1 Sam. 3:13 and note). The Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls add, “He would not hurt Amnon because he was his eldest son and he loved him.” Whether original or not, the sentence accurately highlights a weakness in David’s handling of his sons (14:24, 33; 1 Kin. 1:6 and notes). It is David’s duty as father and as king to “administer justice and equity to all his people” (8:15 and note). His failure to do this contributes to the greatest political crisis of his life—Absalom’s rebellion. One of Absalom’s complaints is that David is slow to provide justice for his people (15:4–6).

This site is some fifteen miles (24 km) north of Jerusalem. Absalom may choose this location to facilitate his imminent escape to relatives in Geshur, across the Jordan River (v. 37).

**Absalom invited all the king’s sons.** The invitation is to participate in the feasting that accompanies the shearing of sheep (cf. 1 Sam. 25:4–8).

verse_quote: let my brother Amnon go with us.
note: Amnon is the oldest son and crown prince, but even so his being singled out by Absalom arouses suspicion. David questions the request: “Why should he go with you?”
David sends not only Amnon but the rest of his sons, perhaps to deter Absalom from taking revenge against Amnon.

In one stroke Absalom will avenge his sister Tamar and move himself closer to the throne (3:3; 15:1–6). He will also become a murderer, repeating his father’s sin as Amnon, also like David, engaged in sexual immorality. David’s sons are demonstrating the same moral failings as their father.
See note on 18:9.
Jonadab seems to know something about Absalom’s plans.

Absalom’s maternal grandfather (3:3).

**Geshur.** See note on v. 23. Absalom flees here to seek the protection of his maternal grandfather (3:3).

verse_quote: the king longed ... the king’s heart went out.
note: It is hard to determine what emotions or reactions precisely are specified in these sentences.
Later known as the birthplace of Amos, Tekoa is a town ten miles (16 km) south of Jerusalem.

verse_quote: the whole clan has risen against your servant.
note: The tale that the wise woman concocts raises not only the issue of blood revenge (v. 11; 3:27; cf. Num. 35:16–25; Deut. 19:11–13; Josh. 20:3) but also the continuance of her family line on its ancestral property, for her enemies propose to execute the surviving son. As she points out, this will leave her with no name or descendant, something that Israelite law seeks to avoid (Deut. 25:5–10). The woman skillfully introduces in her fictional story the same dilemma that David has. His duty to avenge the blood of Amnon conflicts with his anxiety that Absalom, now presumably his heir, not be cut off. Cf. Nathan’s parable in 12:1–4.
The woman is either expressing her willingness to shoulder whatever blame might arise or is requesting, in polite court language, permission to speak further (1 Sam. 25:24).

The woman requests and secures an oath from David, in the name of the Lord, that “the avenger of blood kill no more.” As was the case in Nathan’s parable (12:1–6), a judgment is elicited from David’s own mouth that will then be used to judge him (v. 13).

verse_quote: God will not take away life, and he devises means.
note: The woman seems to mean that God does not desire to take away lives but is ready to see the banishment ended. Some translations read, “God will not take away the life of someone who arranges for a banishment to end.”

While the woman has accomplished her objective of pleading for Absalom, she now returns to the matter of her son, perhaps hoping that David will continue to believe her story and not discover that she and Joab have conspired together (vv. 1–3)., 16
The woman flatters David by praising his judgment. See also v. 20; 19:27; cf. 1 Sam. 29:9.
See note on 13:37.

verse_quote: he is not to come into my presence.
note: David allows Absalom to return to Jerusalem, but the estrangement continues.

As with Saul before him, Absalom is described in exclusively physical terms (1 Sam. 9:1, 2 and notes).

**14:25 blemish.** The term is used of people who are unacceptable to serve in the priesthood (Lev. 21:17–21).

**14:26 he weighed the hair of his head.** The weight of his hair is about five pounds (2.3 kg). The description of how his hair is cut and weighed not only hints at Absalom’s vanity but also foreshadows the way he will die (18:9–15).

See note on 18:18.

**daughter whose name was Tamar.** That only the daughter’s name is recorded is sometimes taken as implying that Absalom’s sons all died young, but the significance of this notice may lie elsewhere. The daughter’s name is the same as the sister whose violation has brought Absalom into conflict with David.
The same amount of time that Absalom waited before taking revenge on Amnon (13:23).

Absalom hopes to win David over, and he does not expect to be executed even if David cannot be assuaged. David has not taken any dire action so far in the affair, and Absalom had some justification for killing Amnon. In effect, his request is that he should be completely punished or completely forgiven and not be left in between.

The narrative ends abruptly. Though David’s action is sometimes referred to as the “kiss of reconciliation,” it is doubtful that a real reconciliation is effected. Ironically, by giving kisses to those who approach him with petitions, Absalom will soon steal away the hearts of the people and launch a rebellion against his father (15:5, 6).

verse_quote: a chariot and horses, and fifty men.
note: See notes on 8:4; 1 Sam. 8:11. Adonijah later does the same thing when he attempts to succeed David on the throne (1 Kin. 1:5).
See note on 13:21.

Four years from the meeting of v. 33 equates to six years from Absalom’s return to Jerusalem (14:28).

**Hebron.** See note on 2:1. Hebron is Absalom’s birthplace (3:2, 3) but also the place where David was first anointed king over Judah (2:4) and subsequently also over Israel (5:3).
See note on 13:23.
Though employing a standard expression (e.g., 1 Sam. 1:17; 20:42; 29:7), David’s farewell to Absalom adds a touch of irony to the story, since Absalom is planning to make war.
See note on v. 7. David first ruled here, and thus Absalom is attempting to usurp the throne in the very heart of David’s power.

See note on 11:3 (“Eliam”).

**Giloh.** A town in the hill country of Judah (Josh. 15:48, 51), probably not far from Hebron.
Heb. “the far house,” perhaps denoting a well-known landmark on the outskirts of the city.

See note on 1 Sam. 30:14. These are David’s bodyguards (1 Sam. 28:2).

**six hundred.** This number, which occurs frequently in military contexts (e.g., Judg. 3:31; 18:11; 20:47; 1 Sam. 13:15), may designate a standard military unit.

**Gittites.** That is, from Gath. Perhaps David won the loyalty of these troops during his time in the Philistine region ruled by Achish of Gath (1 Sam. 27).
This foreigner becomes one of David’s trusted military commanders, alongside Joab and Abishai (vv. 21, 22; 18:2, 5, 12).
Presumably this is to be understood figuratively, not literally, and consequently refers to a recent action.

David’s song of praise (which appears also in Ps. 18, with minor variations) and the prayer of Hannah form a fitting frame for the books of 1 and 2 Samuel (1 Sam. 2:1–10 note). David’s song focuses on the Lord’s deliverance of David. It may be outlined as follows: introductory praise of God as “savior” (vv. 2–4); the psalmist’s distress (vv. 5, 6); the psalmist’s petition (v. 7); the Lord’s response in cosmic demonstration (vv. 8–16) and personal rescue (vv. 17–20); the psalmist’s innocence (vv. 21–25) and the Lord’s faithfulness (vv. 26–30); the Lord’s deliverance (vv. 31–37) and the psalmist’s resultant victories (vv. 38–46); concluding praise of God as Savior (vv. 47–51). Ps. 144, also ascribed to David, shows many similarities in theme and language. This verse is the title or superscription to this song of David, and it is nearly identical to the heading of Ps. 18.

**oracle.** Or “utterance.” The Hebrew word is often, though not exclusively, associated with prophecy (e.g., 1 Sam. 2:30; 2 Kin. 9:26), an association not inappropriate for David (v. 2 and note; Acts 2:30).

**the sweet psalmist of Israel.** Another translation of the Hebrew is “the beloved of Israel’s protector.”

The Lord revealed to David the essential character and glorious benefits of the ideal theocratic king. Only in Christ, the greater Son of David, will such qualities of character be fully displayed and such benefits fully realized (7:4–17 note).

**23:2 The Spirit of the LORD speaks by me.** Other references to David acting or speaking under divine inspiration include 1 Chr. 28:9–19; Matt. 22:43; Acts 1:16; 4:25. David’s empowerment by the Spirit is recounted in 1 Sam. 16:13.

See v. 32; notes on 22:2; 1 Sam. 2:2.

**justly.** Righteous rule is possible only for one who lives in a right relationship with God. On what it means to “fear” God, see note on 1 Sam. 12:14.

verse_quote: the morning light ... sun shining forth.
note: The benefits of righteous rule are enlightenment, fruitfulness, and refreshment. For a fuller development of similar themes, see Ps. 72.

verse_quote: does not my house stand so with God.
note:
David’s confidence rests not in his own righteousness but in the everlasting covenant made with him by a gracious God (7:11–16; 2 Chr. 13:5; 21:7; Ps. 89:3, 4, 28, 29; Is. 55:3; Ezek. 37:25, 26).

**covenant.** Refers to 2 Sam. 7:4–17.
The Hebrew term is “Belial”; see note on 1 Sam. 2:12. The focus here may be on those who have opposed the rule of David.

The presentation of David’s “mighty men” in these verses forms a counterpart to the much shorter description of Davidic champions in 21:15–22. According to v. 39, the warriors listed should total thirty-seven. They are presented in two sets of three (vv. 8–12 and 13–17), plus Abishai (vv. 18, 19), Benaiah (vv. 20–23), and the thirty-one listed in vv. 24–39. However, the “three” of vv. 13–17 are apparently to be counted among “the thirty” (v. 13; v. 24 note) and not separately. Thus, this list contains thirty-six mighty men, and Joab makes thirty-seven. A similar list is given in 1 Chr. 11:10–47 with more than fifteen additional names and no summary total.

**23:8 eight hundred.** 1 Chr. 11:11 has “300,” possibly a copyist’s error. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues.

verse_quote: The LORD brought about a great victory that day.
note: This statement, repeated in v. 12, serves as a reminder that whatever the heroic qualities of the human agent, it is God who ultimately brings victory (8:6, 14; cf. 1 Sam. 14:15, 23; 19:5).
Destroying crops is a common tactic of war (Judg. 6:3–6, 11).
See note on 5:18.
See note on 1 Sam. 23:14.

LORD**.** The brave exploit of the three men is a testimony to their devotion to David, while David’s refusal to drink (v. 17) what has been procured at such great risk to his loyal followers is testimony to his love for them.
See note on 2:18.
See note on 8:18.
David’s bodyguard is presumably composed of Cherethites and Pelethites (1 Sam. 30:14 note).

See note on 2:18.

**the thirty.** “Thirty” may be a round number. Not surprisingly, more of David’s men are from the tribe of Judah than from any other.

**Elhanan.** He is not necessarily the same Elhanan as in 21:19 (note).

verse_quote: Gibeah of the people of Benjamin.
note: David receives support even from Saul’s hometown (1 Sam. 10:26; 11:4).
Not the same as Benaiah in vv. 20–23.
See note on 11:3.
See note on 8:3.
See note on 4:3.

By concluding the list of David’s mighty men with Uriah, the victim of David’s great sin in ch. 11, the chapter ends with a poignant reminder that David is, like all men, a sinner and in need of God’s forgiveness (ch. 12). This theme is continued in the next chapter.

**thirty-seven in all.** See note on vv. 8–39.

This chapter is a fitting conclusion to the books of Samuel. David is shown for what he is, a sinner, but a sinner who is ready to repent and to cast himself upon God’s mercy (12:13 and note). Another appropriate note on which to end these books is the association of the threshing floor of Araunah (vv. 18–25) with Mount Moriah, the future site of the temple (Gen. 22:2; 1 Chr. 22:1; 2 Chr. 3:1).

**24:1 Again.** If a specific occasion is in view, a probable one is the famine of 21:1.

**he incited David.** The antecedent of “he” is the Lord (cf. 1 Sam. 26:19). According to 1 Chr. 21:1, however, it is Satan who moves David. At issue here is the mystery of the presence and practice of evil. The Scripture is clear that God is not the author of evil (James 1:13–15), but it also teaches that the wicked acts of men and of Satan do not fall outside God’s sovereign determination.

**number Israel and Judah.** Taking a census does not appear to be wrong in itself (Num. 1:1, 2; 4:1, 2; 26:1–4), but see Ex. 30:11, 12. This act of census may point to a lack of trust on David’s part, or even to a desire to gain control of God’s providence by making an inventory of His apparent resources. That the report (v. 9) emphasizes military strength may suggest that David wants to take more territory than what the Lord has granted him.
A proverbial expression for all the land.
The reason for Joab’s reluctance is not stated. It can as easily be political as religious, since the people might take a census as a sign that David plans to raise taxes or draft more soldiers.
These verses indicate that the census is begun in the south, east of the Jordan River, and continues in a counterclockwise direction through the land, finally arriving in Beersheba.
Most of this time is needed for taking the census; the travel itself can be accomplished in a matter of weeks.

verse_quote: in Israel there were 800,000 ... Judah were 500,000.
note: 1 Chr. 21:5 has “1,100,000” and “470,000,” respectively. On this difference, see notes on 1 Chr. 21:5 and Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues. The Hebrew word for one thousand can mean “unit,” and therefore the figures may indicate that there are eight hundred military units in Israel and five hundred military units in Judah.

It is uncertain precisely when David’s plea for forgiveness is granted, but perhaps God does it before Gad’s arrival (vv. 11–13). Nevertheless, as in the case of David’s sin against Uriah and Bathsheba, forgiveness does not mean that sin will have no further consequences (v. 13; 12:13, 14). What is David’s sin? Perhaps it is pride that he has such a large army or that he puts his hope in the size of his army rather than in the Lord.
See 1 Sam. 22:5.
The Lord sends Gad to confront David, just as He earlier sent the prophet Nathan (12:1 and note).

Implicit in the threat of pursuit by foes is loss of life by the sword, as 1 Chr. 21:12 makes explicit. Famine, sword, and plague are the OT’s triad of woes regularly threatened for impenitent covenant breaking (Lev. 26:23–26; Deut. 28:21–26; 32:24, 25; 1 Kin. 8:37; 2 Chr. 20:9; Is. 51:19; Jer. 14:12; Ezek. 6:11, 12).

verse_quote: Let us fall into the hand of the
note: LORD**.** Technically, this allows either the first or third option, that is, famine or plague. The inference is sometimes made that David’s choice is selfish, but all three options, including flight before enemies, will cost lives (v. 13 note). David’s motivation is entirely different, for he has learned that the Lord’s mercy is great (v. 16; cf. Ex. 34:6, 7; Neh. 9:17; Pss. 30:5; 86:14–16; 103:8–10; Is. 54:7, 8; 60:10; Hos. 11:8, 9; Joel 2:13).
See v. 2.

LORD**.** See note on Gen. 16:7. On the Lord’s angels as agents of judgment, see Ex. 33:2; Ps. 35:5, 6; Matt. 13:41; Acts 12:23.

**threshing floor of Araunah.** See note on 24:1–25.

verse_quote: let your hand be against me.
note: The heart of David, like the heart of God (v. 16), is grieved by the suffering he sees among his people, his “sheep.” As their shepherd-king, he is moved to compassion and, not knowing that God in His mercy has already stayed His hand (vv. 16, 21), asks that the hand of judgment fall upon him alone. David deserves punishment for his sin, and the people are innocent. David’s offer as a guilty person to suffer in the place of innocent “sheep” is not a very close analogy to Christ’s death for the sake of His sheep (John 10:11), although the language is similar. Unlike David, Christ was personally innocent and died for the guilty.
See note on 1 Sam. 10:8.

verse_quote: I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing.
note:
While God’s grace and forgiveness are free, David understands that proper worship of God is never to be cheap or careless (cf. Mal. 1:6–14; 2 Cor. 8:1–5). The consistent testimony of Scripture is that God deserves our best, the “firstfruits” (Num. 18:12; Deut. 18:3–5; 26:10; Neh. 12:44; Prov. 3:9).

**fifty shekels of silver.** 1 Chr. 21:25 records a much larger sum of six hundred shekels of gold, possibly referring to a larger transaction of which the fifty shekels is a part.

verse_quote: David built there an altar to the
note:
LORD**.** According to 1 Chr. 22:1, this is the location for the future Solomonic temple.

**burnt offerings and peace offerings.** See note on 1 Sam. 10:8.

**the LORD responded to the plea for the land.** An almost identical statement is made in 21:14.
